subject: Gastrointestinal
subtopic: Microscopic colitis and irritable bowel syndrome
vignette: A 66-year-old woman presents with 6 months of chronic watery diarrhea. She has no weight loss or hematochezia. Colonoscopy shows normal-appearing colonic mucosa. Biopsies show a lymphocytic infiltrate in the lamina propria with intraepithelial lymphocytosis.
question: Which diagnosis best fits these findings?

options.text: Ulcerative colitis with continuous inflammation from the rectum
Irritable bowel syndrome with altered stool frequency and form
Microscopic colitis with lymphocytic infiltrate and normal endoscopy
Crohn disease with noncaseating granulomas
Collagenous sprue with villous atrophy of the small bowel

explanation_correct: Microscopic colitis causes chronic watery diarrhea, most often in older females, and is characterized by normal-appearing mucosa on endoscopy. Histology shows either lymphocytic infiltration of the lamina propria with intraepithelial lymphocytosis or a thickened subepithelial collagen band (collagenous colitis). There is no gross inflammation, bleeding, or structural abnormality.

explanation_incorrect.A: Ulcerative colitis would show continuous inflamed, friable mucosa with crypt abscesses on endoscopy and is not associated with a normal-appearing colon.
explanation_incorrect.B: Irritable bowel syndrome causes abdominal pain related to defecation and changes in stool frequency or form but has no histologic lymphocytic infiltrate.
explanation_incorrect.D: Crohn disease shows skip lesions, transmural inflammation, and noncaseating granulomas rather than a normal-appearing mucosa with lymphocytosis.
explanation_incorrect.E: Collagenous sprue affects the small bowel with villous atrophy and malabsorption rather than causing watery diarrhea with a normal colonoscopy.

educationalObjective: Microscopic colitis causes chronic watery diarrhea in older females with normal endoscopy and diagnostic histology.

subject: Gastrointestinal
subtopic: Microscopic colitis and irritable bowel syndrome
vignette: A 32-year-old woman reports recurrent abdominal pain for 9 months. The pain is relieved by defecation and associated with both looser stools and occasional constipation. Evaluation shows no structural abnormalities, and she also reports symptoms of anxiety.
question: Which diagnostic feature is characteristic of irritable bowel syndrome?

options.text: Bloody diarrhea with fever and leukocytosis
Abdominal pain that is unrelated to defecation and worsens at night
Noncaseating granulomas on intestinal biopsy
Recurrent abdominal pain associated with defecation and changes in stool frequency or form, without structural disease
Loss of haustra and a lead-pipe appearance on imaging

explanation_correct: Irritable bowel syndrome is defined by recurrent abdominal pain associated with at least two of the following: related to defecation, change in stool frequency, and change in stool form. There are no structural abnormalities. It is most common in middle-aged females, may be diarrhea-predominant, constipation-predominant, or mixed, and is associated with fibromyalgia and mood disorders.

explanation_incorrect.A: Bloody diarrhea with fever suggests inflammatory or infectious disease, not IBS, which has no inflammatory findings.
explanation_incorrect.B: Pain unrelated to defecation or waking the patient at night is a red flag that argues against IBS and should prompt evaluation for organic disease.
explanation_incorrect.C: Noncaseating granulomas indicate Crohn disease rather than a functional disorder.
explanation_incorrect.E: Loss of haustra with a lead-pipe colon is the radiographic hallmark of long-standing ulcerative colitis.

educationalObjective: IBS is a functional disorder with pain related to defecation and stool changes but no structural abnormalities.

subject: Gastrointestinal
subtopic: Microscopic colitis and irritable bowel syndrome
vignette: A 29-year-old woman with abdominal pain and alternating diarrhea and constipation has a normal colonoscopy. Her physician is trying to determine whether this represents irritable bowel syndrome or mild inflammatory bowel disease before starting treatment.
question: Which finding would most strongly favor an inflammatory rather than a functional disorder?

options.text: Symptoms that improve with dietary fiber and lifestyle modification
A history of fibromyalgia and depression
Normal stool frequency between symptomatic flares
Absence of weight loss or nocturnal symptoms
Elevated fecal calprotectin

explanation_correct: Fecal calprotectin is used to monitor inflammatory bowel disease activity and to distinguish inflammatory disease from noninflammatory disorders such as irritable bowel syndrome. An elevated value supports active intestinal inflammation even when endoscopy appears normal, prompting closer evaluation for microscopic colitis or IBD.

explanation_incorrect.A: Improvement with lifestyle and dietary change is consistent with IBS, the first-line treatment for which is lifestyle modification and dietary changes.
explanation_incorrect.B: Fibromyalgia and mood disorders are associations of IBS and do not indicate an inflammatory disorder.
explanation_incorrect.C: Normal stool frequency between flares is compatible with a functional disorder rather than persistent inflammation.
explanation_incorrect.D: Absence of weight loss and nocturnal symptoms is reassuring against organic disease and supports a functional etiology.

educationalObjective: Elevated fecal calprotectin supports intestinal inflammation and distinguishes IBD from irritable bowel syndrome.

subject: Gastrointestinal
subtopic: Microscopic colitis and irritable bowel syndrome
vignette: A 34-year-old woman is diagnosed with diarrhea-predominant irritable bowel syndrome after a normal evaluation. She asks about the initial approach to management.
question: Which intervention is recommended as first-line therapy?

options.text: Lifestyle modification and dietary changes
Immediate colectomy for refractory symptoms
Systemic glucocorticoids to suppress intestinal inflammation
Broad-spectrum antibiotics for presumed bacterial overgrowth
Intravenous infliximab to block tumor necrosis factor

explanation_correct: First-line treatment of irritable bowel syndrome is lifestyle modification and dietary changes. The condition is chronic, with diarrhea-predominant, constipation-predominant, and mixed patterns, and is associated with fibromyalgia and mood disorders. There is no structural abnormality to treat surgically or with immunosuppression.

explanation_incorrect.B: Colectomy has no role in a functional disorder without structural disease and would be reserved for severe refractory inflammatory disease.
explanation_incorrect.C: Glucocorticoids treat active inflammatory bowel disease; there is no documented intestinal inflammation in IBS.
explanation_incorrect.D: Antibiotics are not first-line therapy for IBS; bacterial overgrowth is a distinct condition diagnosed with breath testing.
explanation_incorrect.E: Infliximab is a biologic used for inflammatory bowel disease, not for a functional disorder with normal mucosa.

educationalObjective: First-line management of IBS is lifestyle modification and dietary change.
